editorial_contributions.text: A \(2\)-coloring of the diagonals (including sides) of a regular convex \(n\)-gon is a circulant coloring of \(K_n\) if all diagonals of the same length have the same color. Corresponding to such colorings are two circulant Ramsey numbers \(RC_1(G,H)\) and \(RC_2(G,H)\) such that for all \(n < RC_1(G,H)\) a circulant coloring without a monochromatic \(G\) or \(H\) exists and for all \(n \geq RC_2\) no such coloring exists. The Ramsey numbers \(RC_1\) and \(RC_2\) are determined for all paths, cycles, graphs on at most five vertices, and for some small complete graphs. As a consequence of the latter results, new lower bounds \(R(K_4,K_{10}) \geq 92\) and \(R(K_5,K_8) \geq 101\) for classical Ramsey numbers are obtained.

Assume that the vertices of the complete graph \(K_n\) are labeled by \(1,2,\dots,n\). A \(2\)-coloring \(\pi\) of the edges \(E_n\) of \(K_n\) is called a distance coloring if for all \((n,m), (k,l)\in E_n\), \(| n-m| =| k-l| \rightarrow \pi(n,m)= \pi(k,l)\). For given graphs \(G\) and \(H\) the distance Ramsey number RD\((G,H)\) is defined as the minimum \(n\) such that every distance coloring of \(K_n\) contains a monochromatic copy of \(G\) or \(H\). In the paper, for small graphs the values of RD\((G,H)\) are determined by computer and some lower bounds of classical Ramsey numbers are improved.

Summary: Triangle and hexagon boards are called \(d\)-Latin boards if the first positive integers are placed into the triangles and hexagons, such that each line with \(\ell\) cells has pairwise different integers being at most \(\ell+d\). Here we ask for the minimum \(d\) of \(d\)-Latin boards.

msc.text: Orthogonal arrays, Latin squares, Room squares
Combinatorial aspects of tessellation and tiling problems

editorial_contributions.text: For the three tessellations of the Euclidean plane by squares, hexagons, and triangles Euclidean gameboards \(B_ n\) are considered. A board \(B_ n\) is called magic if the numbers from 1 to the number of cells of \(B_ n\) are placed into the cells such that all line sums are \(m(n)\), the magic constant. There is a rich literature on square magic gameboards. In the paper under review some triangle and hexagon magic gameboards are presented. If a magic gameboard \(B_ n\) does not exist, the minimum \(d(n)\) is discussed such that there is an arrangement with all line sums being integers in the interval \([m(n)-d(n), m(n)+d(n)]\).

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: For gameboards as parts of the three Euclidean tessellations of the plane we introduce fair magic arrangements of the numbers \(1,2,\dots\) where the average of the numbers in each of the parallel lines is equal to the average of all numbers.

Summary: The chessboard Ramsey number \(r=r(G,H)\) is the minimum number \(r\) such that every two-coloring (green and red) of the sides of the squares of the \(r \times r\)-chessboard contains a green \(G\) or a red \(H\). The existence is possible only for \(G\) being a path \(P_3\) or \(P_4\) and for \(H\) being a certain tree. The exact values of \(r(P_3,P_k)\) and the values for \(r(P_3,H)\) and \(r(P_4, H)\) for all small graphs \(H\) are determined and the existence of \(r(P_4,P_k)\) is proved.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1034.52002].
